result:
**Solution 2 is the only one whose argument holds up under the most literal reading of the problem.** I can't confirm its answer against a reference, though, because the problem doesn't specify how the layers are offset.

**The model.** Every brick is identical, and nothing says the layers are staggered, so the literal reading is that all layers are flush on the left and bricks in every layer sit at the same integer grid positions. Then the bottom side of brick $i$ in layer $n$ lies exactly on the top side of brick $i$ in layer $n+1$, and no other brick touches it along a segment of positive length. Each move is forced, and there is exactly one path to layer 2026.

**Solution 1** assumes each brick touches two bricks below, with index map $i \to \{i, i+1\}$. That requires a half-brick stagger that the problem never states. Its own recurrence also ignores the fact that layer $n+1$ has about twice as many bricks as layer $n$, so the claimed adjacency is not consistent with the stated brick counts. Its final number $2^{2025}$ is plausible as an arithmetic value, but the model behind it is unjustified.

**Solution 3** is internally inconsistent. Under any model where the top brick touches at least one brick in layer 2, the count to layer 2 should match its own recurrence. Its formula $\binom{n-1}{\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor}$ gives 1 at $n=2$, which does not match its stated two-neighbour adjacency. The recurrence and the closed form do not agree.

**Solution 2** states its geometric assumptions explicitly, checks that only one brick is shared between consecutive layers, and correctly observes that the index $i \le 2^n-1 < 2^{n+1}-1$ always exists. Its argument is complete under that model.

CHOICE: 2
